intro: Six of these seven stand on Mont-Royal, in the park or in the two cemeteries sharing its flank, so Montreal arrives here as a mountain rather than a city. The seventh waits at the foot of the hill on a McGill lawn, a ginkgo that a botanist who has spent twenty-five years looking picked as the most remarkable tree in the city. Up top: an Austrian pine that grew eighteen metres wide instead of tall, a silver maple that stood on a florist's field before the graves arrived, and one of the last big American elms in Montreal.
meta_description: Seven remarkable trees in Montreal, six of them on Mont-Royal: a pine wider than it is tall, a 5.8 metre silver maple, one of the last big elms.
question_meta: Montreal's oldest tree is a red oak on Mont-Royal, roughly 200 years old and seeded before the park existed. Where it stands, and six more.
question_answer: The oldest tree on this page is a northern red oak in Parc du Mont-Royal, standing off a secondary trail leading from the Olmsted Trail. The city's own dendrological survey measured it at 118 centimetres across the trunk at chest height and 200 centimetres at the base, and reads that as roughly two hundred years, which makes it one of the ten largest oaks on the mountain. It seeded itself rather than being planted, and it was already mature when the park was laid out around it in 1876. In 1954 Mayor Jean Drapeau had much of the mountain's undergrowth cleared in a campaign remembered afterwards as the morality cuts, and this oak came through that too. Two things are worth knowing before you go. It stands in a stand of white spruce about fifty years old, which makes the age difference obvious the moment you are standing there. And it is not in good health: a primary branch tore out and left a major cavity in the trunk, and the city's survey describes it as being in the twilight of its life, which is a formal way of saying go sooner rather than later.
question_context: There is no national or provincial register of remarkable trees behind this page. What Montreal has instead is unusual and better: the Ville de Montreal publishes a dendrological page for individual designated trees on Mont-Royal and in the two cemeteries on its flank, carrying species, trunk diameter at chest height and at the base, an age reading and a paragraph of history. Six of the seven trees here rest on that source alone, which is why each of those pages says so in plain words and carries a flag; only the McGill ginkgo has two independent accounts. Every pin on this city is marked approximate, and that is not modesty: the source places a tree in a cemetery section or along a trail rather than on a spot, so the prose carries the findable detail instead, a plot number, a gate, a parking area. One tree that was on the original list is not here. The cemetery's designated red ash was felled in 2025 to the emerald ash borer, which we learned because its own page now redirects to an address ending in disparu. See the full list of seven on the Montreal page.

faq.q: What is the oldest tree in Montreal?
faq.a: The oldest on this page is a northern red oak in Parc du Mont-Royal, put at roughly two hundred years by the city's own survey and one of the ten largest oaks on the mountain. It seeded itself and was already mature when the park was laid out in 1876. It is in poor health, with a major cavity where a primary branch tore out.

faq.q: Can I see them all in one walk?
faq.a: Almost. Six of the seven are on Mont-Royal, split between the park and the two adjoining cemeteries, Mount Royal Cemetery and Notre-Dame-des-Neiges, which is a long but real walk. The McGill ginkgo is downtown at the foot of the same hill and fits naturally at the start or the end of it.

faq.q: Can you visit the cemetery trees?
faq.a: Yes. Mount Royal Cemetery and Notre-Dame-des-Neiges are both open to visitors during the day and free to walk through. They are large, though, so the plot numbers and gates named on each tree's page matter more here than the map pin does.

faq.q: Why do the pins say approximate?
faq.a: Because the source is honest about it and so are we. The city's tree pages place a specimen in a cemetery section or along a named trail rather than at a coordinate, so marking these pins confirmed would be inventing a precision nobody has. Each page carries the most findable detail there is instead.

trees.name: The McGill Law Ginkgo

location.address: McGill University Faculty of Law grounds, corner of Peel Street and Doctor Penfield Avenue, Montreal

trees.story:
Asked to name the most remarkable tree in Montreal, a botanist who has spent twenty-five years looking for them picked this one, standing on a lawn beside the McGill law faculty.

Suzanne Hardy's case for it is partly the tree and partly who put it there. She believes it is likely the first ginkgo of its kind planted in Montreal, and that it went in about 120 years ago at the hands of the Olmsted family. Frederick Law Olmsted laid out Mont-Royal Park, the hill this ginkgo sits at the foot of, so the tree and the mountain above it come from the same drawing office. Six of the seven trees on this page are up on that hill. This one waits at the bottom of it.

The age is her estimate rather than a measurement. Nobody has published a girth, there is no plaque, and the pin marks the corner of Peel Street and Doctor Penfield Avenue rather than the trunk itself; the Chancellor Day Hall grounds are open to walk through and it is not a large lawn.

Ginkgos are the last surviving species of an order that otherwise ended with the dinosaurs, and they keep the habits. This one holds its leaves green into late autumn, turns them a hard uniform yellow, then drops very nearly the whole crown inside a couple of days. Arrive in the wrong week and you get a green tree or a bare one.

best_time.label: late October, when the whole crown turns gold and drops within days

trees.access: Free, on open McGill University campus grounds; the law faculty's outdoor grounds are publicly walkable
trees.transport: McGill or Peel metro station, roughly 10-15 minute walk uphill
trees.how_to_recognise: On the lawn beside Chancellor Day Hall, at the foot of the hill. The lawn is small and the fan-shaped ginkgo leaves are unmistakable.

trees.name: The Bicentennial Red Oak of Mont-Royal

location.address: Parc du Mont-Royal, along a secondary trail off the Olmsted Trail, in a stand of roughly 50-year-old white spruce, Ville-Marie borough

trees.story:
In 1954 Mayor Jean Drapeau had much of Mont-Royal's undergrowth cut away, in a campaign remembered afterwards as the morality cuts. This oak came through it.

It is one of the ten largest oaks on the mountain: 118 centimetres across the trunk at chest height, 200 at the base, which the city's dendrological survey reads as roughly two hundred years. That measurement was taken in 2011, so the tree is somewhat wider now than the number says and the age band runs correspondingly wide. It seeded itself here rather than being planted, and it was already mature when the park was laid out around it in 1876.

You find it in a stand of white spruce about fifty years old, which makes the arithmetic obvious the moment you are standing there. Everything in sight arrived four generations after the oak did.

It is not in good health. A primary branch tore out and left a major cavity in the trunk, and the survey describes the tree as being in the twilight of its life, which is a formal way of saying go sooner rather than later. It stands off a secondary trail leading from the Olmsted Trail, and that trail is the practical instruction, because the pin is approximate. The city of Montreal's own heritage page for the mountain is the only published account of this tree; nobody else has written it up.
trees.access: Free, in the publicly open Parc du Mont-Royal, accessible daily, no gate or ticket
trees.transport: Mont-Royal metro station, then roughly a 25-30 minute uphill walk via the park's trail network toward the Olmsted Trail area (or a shorter ride if using the park's own shuttle/bus service)
trees.how_to_recognise: A big oak standing in a stand of white spruce roughly fifty years old, off a secondary trail leading from the Olmsted Trail. A primary branch has torn out and left a major cavity in the trunk.

trees.name: The Great Yew of Mount Royal Cemetery

location.address: Mount Royal Cemetery (Cimetiere Mont-Royal), standing isolated on a gentle slope with sparse gravestones, Outremont/Cote-des-Neiges side of the mountain

trees.story:
A Japanese yew in this climate normally manages five or six metres. This one is fifteen.

It stands on its own on a gentle slope in Mount Royal Cemetery, in a stretch where the gravestones are thinly scattered, which is what makes it findable and also what makes it worth the walk: a yew given room to become a tree instead of a hedge. The city's survey calls it the largest of its species on the mountain, at 50 centimetres across the trunk, which for a yew is a great deal of wood.

Some specialists think it is not one plant at all. The bark is oddly reddish and the crown unusually round and compact, and the theory on the record is that a male and a female were grafted together and grew on as a single tree. Nobody has taken it apart to find out.

Its age is given as over sixty years, which makes it the youngest tree on this page and does nothing to explain the height.

One caution about the address, because two cemeteries adjoin on this flank of the mountain and there is a Japanese yew recorded in the other one as well. This is the Mount Royal Cemetery tree, not the Notre-Dame-des-Neiges one. Enter from the chemin de la Foret side. The city's heritage page for it is the only published description that exists.
trees.access: Free; Mount Royal Cemetery is an active, operating cemetery open to the public during its posted daily visiting hours
trees.transport: Edouard-Montpetit metro station, roughly 15-20 minute walk; or enter via the chemin de la Foret / chemin Remembrance side of the cemetery
trees.how_to_recognise: A yew fifteen metres tall, standing alone on a gentle slope among thinly scattered gravestones. The adjoining cemetery has a Japanese yew too: this is the Mount Royal Cemetery one, entered from the chemin de la Foret side.

trees.name: The Wide Pine at the Cemetery Gate

location.address: Notre-Dame-des-Neiges Cemetery, center of the large open area at the main entrance, Cote-des-Neiges - Notre-Dame-de-Grace borough

trees.story:
This pine is 7.5 metres tall and 18 metres wide. It has spent about 150 years growing sideways.

It sits in the middle of the open ground just inside the main gate of Notre-Dame-des-Neiges, which makes it the easiest tree on this page to find. Walk in and it is the thing in front of you, shaped rather more like a mushroom than a pine. The trunk is 85 centimetres across at chest height and 97 at the base.

It was planted deliberately, and early. Between about 1870 and 1872 the cemetery's administration bought thousands of trees to landscape the new pathways during its first phase of development, and this Austrian pine was one of them. That makes it part of the cemetery's opening gesture rather than something that turned up later, and it has been marking the entrance ever since, through every funeral that has come through the gate behind it.

Look at the trunk closely and it is punched with small round holes, the work of a woodpecker going after what lives under the bark. The tree does not appear to mind.

Everything known about it comes from one place, the city of Montreal's own dendrological page for this specimen. No outside source has published a word about it, which for a tree standing in plain sight at the gate of Canada's busiest cemetery is a strange gap.
trees.access: Free; Notre-Dame-des-Neiges is an active, operating cemetery open to the public during its posted daily visiting hours
trees.transport: Cote-des-Neiges metro station, roughly 15 minute walk to the main gate
trees.how_to_recognise: The easiest on this page. Walk in the main gate of Notre-Dame-des-Neiges and it is the thing in front of you, wider than it is tall and shaped more like a mushroom than a pine.

trees.name: The Last Elm of Mont-Royal

location.address: Parc du Mont-Royal, near the Smith House parking area, on the margin of the property adjacent to the Olmsted Trail, Ville-Marie borough

trees.story:
Montreal once had roughly 22,000 American elms. Dutch elm disease took very nearly all of them. This is one of the few still standing.

It grows on the margin of the Smith House property in Parc du Mont-Royal, on the edge next to the Olmsted Trail, and at 110 centimetres across the trunk and 128 at the base it is the largest American elm documented anywhere in the park. The city's survey reads those measurements as roughly 120 years, and the measuring was done some years ago, so add what it has grown since. It appears to have seeded itself rather than been planted, which is now an unusual biography for an elm: the ones that were planted were mostly along streets, and the streets are where the disease moved fastest.

What nobody can promise is that it will still be here. The disease has not gone anywhere, it travels between elms through root grafts and beetles, and a tree this size is a target rather than a fortress. The city's own heritage page is the only published record of this elm, and it has not been marked as lost, which is the most recent evidence there is that the tree is alive.

Treat that as a reason to go this season rather than next. If you get there and it is gone, tell us and we will take it down.
trees.access: Free, in the publicly open Parc du Mont-Royal, accessible daily, no gate or ticket
trees.transport: Mont-Royal metro station, then roughly a 20-25 minute uphill walk to Smith House via the park's trail network
trees.how_to_recognise: On the margin of the Smith House property, on the edge beside the Olmsted Trail. A mature American elm is a rare thing here, which is most of how you know it.

trees.name: The McKenna Silver Maple

location.address: Notre-Dame-des-Neiges Cemetery, southeast section (plot ND 7002-9030), near chemin de la Cote-des-Neiges and chemin Remembrance, bordering a burial island

trees.story:
This tree was here before the cemetery was. It grew on a florist's private grounds, and the graves came later.

Patrick McKenna arrived in Montreal from Ireland in 1847 and by 1851 had founded what is described as Canada's oldest florist house. The silver maple stood as an ornamental on his own horticultural property while that ground was still his field. Notre-Dame-des-Neiges incorporated in 1907, five years before he died, and the burial sections were laid out around the trunk.

Nobody wrote down the year he planted it, so the honest range is somewhere inside his sixty years on the land, which comes out at roughly 150 years. What is measured rather than inferred is the trunk: 185 centimetres across at chest height, 191 at the base, a girth of 5.8 metres. That is the second-thickest tree in the cemetery and comfortably the largest on this page.

It is in the southeast section, plot ND 7002-9030, near where chemin de la Cote-des-Neiges meets chemin Remembrance, on the edge of a burial island. The plot number is the useful part of that address: the map pin will get you to the right corner of a very large cemetery, and the number gets you the rest of the way.

The city of Montreal's survey of the mountain is the only published account of this maple.
trees.access: Free; Notre-Dame-des-Neiges is an active, operating cemetery open to the public during its posted daily visiting hours
trees.transport: Cote-des-Neiges metro station, roughly 15 minute walk to the main gate, then a further walk within the grounds to the southeast section
trees.how_to_recognise: Plot ND 7002-9030 is the useful address: the pin gets you to the right corner of a very large cemetery and the plot number gets you the rest of the way. It is the thickest tree in sight, 5.8 metres round.

trees.name: The Honey Locust of Section B

location.address: Notre-Dame-des-Neiges Cemetery, plot section B, Cote-des-Neiges - Notre-Dame-de-Grace borough

trees.story:
The way this tree's age was worked out is that somebody read the gravestone beside it. The planting matches a death date inscribed there, which makes it a private act of commemoration by one family, and a lovely but slightly shaky way to date a tree.

Taken at face value it puts the honey locust at roughly a hundred years, give or take a decade either way. The city's survey recorded it at eighty to ninety years in 2011, so add the years since. The trunk is 65 centimetres across and 81 at the base, which made it the largest of the eleven honey locusts scattered through Notre-Dame-des-Neiges when the count was taken.

The crown is the odd part. It is displaced and asymmetrical, the whole weight of it thrown off to one side toward the dome of Saint-Joseph's Oratory on the horizon, and a long scar runs where a large branch came away. Honey locust resists rot and tolerates city air better than most trees, which is why it turns up on so many streets and why one can carry an injury like that for decades.

The address is section B, and that is as precise as the record gets, so allow time. The city's dendrological page for it is the only published description of this tree anywhere.
trees.access: Free; Notre-Dame-des-Neiges is an active, operating cemetery open to the public during its posted daily visiting hours
trees.transport: Cote-des-Neiges metro station, roughly 15 minute walk to the main gate, then a further walk within the grounds to section B
trees.how_to_recognise: The crown is thrown right off to one side, toward the dome of Saint-Joseph's Oratory, with a long scar where a big branch came away. Section B is as precise as the record gets, so allow time.
